source: Schmied, Bornschein, Grau-Moya, Wulfmeier, Pascanu (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities
finding: Gemma2 2B, 9B and 27B in Gaussian bandits stop exploring early. Small models copy the most frequent action (frequency bias). Large models drop that bias but turn greedy. Models know the right rule but do not act on it (knowing-doing gap). A coded 'try each arm once' step gave the biggest gain; RL fine-tuning with a +1 bonus for untried actions raised coverage.
numbers: 10 arms, 64 parallel envs: action coverage 40% (2B) and 65% (9B, 27B) with CoT; 25% without CoT. 20 arms: largest models cover only 45%. Frequency bias: 96% repeat share for 2B vs 14% for 27B. Knowing-doing: 87% of rationales correct, yet greedy action chosen 58% vs optimal 21% (the intro says 64%). RLFT on 2B: coverage +12%; with the +1 untried-action bonus coverage 50% -> 70%. Try-all prompt: 27B almost closes the gap to UCB.
quote: LLMs often know how to solve a task but fail at acting on this knowledge
limits: Gemma2 family only (no reasoning models); 50 steps; stateless bandits; the 58% vs 64% figure differs between text sections. The fine-tuning result is not a scaffold result.
agent_relevance: Size does not fix greed: it swaps frequency bias (small) for greed (large). A coded forced first sweep of every probe (try-all) beat every other prompt-level fix, which supports a coded probe tally and a minimum-coverage rule in S3.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Comparing Exploration-Exploitation Strategies of LLMs and Humans: Insights from Standard Multi-armed Bandit Experiments
finding: LLMs, humans and bandit algorithms were fitted with the same choice model (directed term, random term, perseveration). Turning thinking on moves LLMs toward the human mix of directed and random exploration in a simple stationary 2-armed task. In a 4-armed non-stationary task even thinking models stay weak at directed exploration.
numbers: Human data: Gershman (2018) N=45 humans, 20 games x 10 rounds, 2-armed; Chakroun et al. (2020) N=31 placebo participants, restless 4-armed, 75 rounds. o3-mini high thinking: directed exploration above the human level and random exploration below it. Gemini-2.5-flash: raising the thinking budget moves directed exploration up to, not beyond, the human level. 4-armed: basic LLMs have uncertainty coefficients that stay negative; thinking raises them but not enough.
limits: Parameter values were read from figure descriptions and prose, not from a table. Model-fit parameters are 'projections' for non-human agents (authors' wording). Models: GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek families including o3-mini and Gemini-2.5-flash.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 5 partly: 2025 reasoning models explore more like humans on easy bandits but still fail directed exploration when the world changes. Thinking budget is a lever on exploration. A coded tally was not tested here.

source: Arumugam & Griffiths (2026, ICLR) Toward Efficient Exploration by Large Language Model Agents
finding: The LLM implements posterior sampling (PSRL) step by step (sample a hypothesis, act on it, update) instead of exploring implicitly. This beats Reflexion and in-context RL on exploration-heavy tasks. A myopic information-directed variant (LLM-IDS) is in an appendix. Reasoning models help every agent but do not close the gap to explicit exploration.
numbers: RiverSwim 3 states: upgrading GPT-4o to o1-mini turns LLM-PSRL from near-linear regret to sub-linear regret on par with classic PSRL; in-context RL finds the optimal policy in just over 25% of trials and 60% fall back to the downstream reward. DeepSeek-R1 (combination lock 20 trials, Wordle 40 trials) improves all agents, but the best baseline with R1 is not significantly better than LLM-PSRL with GPT-4o. LLM-IDS on the informative-action bandit K=10, 10 trials: recovers the optimal probe-first strategy exactly; LLM-PSRL cannot. Tokens: PSRL used more tokens in combination lock (GPT-4o enumerates the whole posterior) but had lower regret when truncated to the same token count.
limits: Small trial counts. LLM-IDS is myopic and is an appendix pilot. The hypothesis set is small enough to enumerate. The token comparison is a figure, not a table.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, 2, 3, 8: a sampled-hypothesis loop with an explicit update step is a workable approximation of expected information gain, and a one-step (myopic) information score already beats sampling-based exploration where one cheap probe reveals the answer. It costs more tokens but wins at equal tokens in the lock task.

source: Harris & Slivkins (2026, UAI) Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit?
finding: Used in silos, LLMs are weak exploitation oracles beyond small tasks and lose to plain linear regression, even with tools and summaries. Reasoning models (GPT-5 family) do best but are slow and costly. LLMs are useful as exploration oracles: they propose good candidate actions in large semantic action spaces for a classic bandit algorithm to test.
numbers: Models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. Exploration tasks: MovieLens recommendations, a large arXiv title-for-abstract task, open-ended philosophical questions with contrarian answers. Authors report robust success across task types, LLMs and prompting strategies.
quote: LLMs are useful as exploration oracles that propose high-quality candidate actions
limits: I did not extract one headline number from the text. Two reasoning models could not be run (context too short). Contextual bandits, not hypothesis probes.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting S3: the LLM proposes candidate probes (what it is good at); code does the scoring, tally and stopping (what it is bad at).

source: Friston, Rigoli, Ognibene, Mathys, FitzGerald, Pezzulo (2015) Active inference and epistemic value. Cognitive Neuroscience 6(4):187-214
finding: Choice is defined as minimising expected free energy, which splits into extrinsic value (expected utility) and epistemic value (expected information gain). Expected utility alone and KL control come out as special cases. Tested only in simulated T-maze trials, not on people or animals. Epistemic value covers curiosity (Bayesian surprise) and an ambiguity term (expected entropy of outcomes given states) that keeps the agent away from locations whose outcomes stay noisy.
numbers: Simulation: 128 trials per setting, six levels of prior preference, four schemes (active inference FE, KL control, expected utility RL, fixed-precision DA). When the utility of the arms is zero, expected-utility and KL schemes fall below chance, while the active-inference scheme still reaches the reward by using the informative cue. No human data. Dopamine claims are simulated precision updates.
quote: Epistemic value is maximized until there is no further information gain, after which exploitation is assured
limits: All claims are simulation. The switch is a property of the maths: the epistemic term decays as uncertainty is resolved. Text came from a two-column PDF with garbled layout; numbers were read from captions and prose only. Not a test of LLMs.
agent_relevance: Replaces the snippet-based claim: the explore-then-exploit switch is in the formulation itself, and an ambiguity term (not only novelty) is part of epistemic value. That is the principled noisy-TV guard. Real use needs a coded gain estimate and an explicit threshold.

source: Friston, Lin, Frith, Pezzulo, Hobson, Ondobaka (2017) Active Inference, Curiosity and Insight. Neural Computation 29:2633-2683
finding: A simulated agent learns an abstract colour rule from a few cue samples. Novelty (information gain about model parameters) draws it to locations that look ambiguous at first; once the rule is learned it avoids them. A second step, Bayesian model reduction (a sleep-like pruning of redundant parameters), produces sudden aha jumps in performance.
numbers: Single agent: 32 trials of 6 epochs each, transition from ignorance to understanding after trial 14. 64 artificial agents: with model reduction nearly all reach 100% around trial 10; chance is about 30%. Some agents need up to 10 trials, so aha timing depends on the data sampled. Predictions only (shorter evoked-response latency after insight, sleep effect). No human experiment was run.
quote: curiosity manifests as an active sampling of the world to minimize uncertainty about hypotheses
limits: Pure simulation with a hand-made hypothesis space that contained the true rule (authors say this avoided a greedy search over models). The authors say human tests are still needed.
agent_relevance: Curiosity is self-limiting here: novelty-driven probing fades as the rule is learned. The insight step (prune the hypothesis space, then commit) matches the S3 to later-state handoff, but it needs a hypothesis space that contains the answer.

source: Zajkowski, Kossut, Wilson (2017) A causal role for right frontopolar cortex in directed, but not random, exploration. eLife 6:e27430
finding: A human follow-up that re-used the Horizon task (Wilson 2014 design). Inhibiting right frontopolar cortex with theta-burst TMS cut directed exploration (information bonus at the long horizon) and left random exploration (decision noise) unchanged. The horizon-dependent information bonus was measurable in a new sample.
numbers: N=31 healthy right-handed adults (19 F, 12 M, ages 19-32); started at 16 and extended to 31 on feedback; within-subject RFPC vs vertex stimulation; 160 games per session, games of 5 or 10 choices, payoff SD 8. Model-based result: information bonus at horizon 6 reduced by about 4.8 points (99% of posterior samples below zero); weak hint at horizon 1 (85%); no effect on decision noise.
limits: Sample size was extended after a first look (optional stopping risk). Bayesian posterior summaries, not p-values. TMS effects may spread to nearby cortex (authors' own caveat). It supports the dissociation, not an effect size for horizon alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partly: a second lab-level dataset in which directed exploration depends on the horizon. For the agent it supports telling it the remaining budget explicitly, because in people the information bonus is driven by the horizon.

source: Timokhov, Timashkov, Zinchenko (2025) No effect of preliminarily simulated cathodal HD-tDCS on the frontopolar cortex in the exploration-exploitation task. Sci Rep
finding: A null result: cathodal HD-tDCS over frontopolar cortex, planned with field simulation, left exploratory behaviour and fNIRS resting-state activity unchanged. The task was a strategy-switching task modelled with the PROBE model, not the Horizon task.
numbers: N=43 right-handed adults (19 M, age 21.1 +- 2.4), within-subject sham vs cathodal one week apart. No difference in task performance curves around the combination switch between conditions. fNIRS showed no physiological effect of stimulation.
limits: Not a replication of directed exploration: different task, and tDCS (weak) rather than TMS. The authors say the protocol may simply not have affected the region.
agent_relevance: A boundary note, not a failed replication of the horizon effect. No failed Horizon-task replication was found in what I could open.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: A stop rule (stop sampling when the leading answer is confident enough) beats a fixed sample budget. It models answer counts with a Beta, Dirichlet or Chinese-restaurant-process prior, so it also works when the number of possible answers is unknown.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs. Up to 7.9x fewer samples with average accuracy drop below 0.1%; confidence threshold 0.95. Reductions 4.4x (GPT-3.5-turbo), 1.9x (Vicuna-13B), 3.4x (code-davinci-002). Example row: code-davinci-002 100 samples at 61.4% vs 23.6 samples at 63.4%. At equal average sample cost, adaptive stopping gave higher accuracy than uniform self-consistency (their Fig. 5). The Beta rule costs about 0.03 ms vs about 95-101 ms for Dirichlet and CRP.
limits: It stops on answer agreement, not on information gain about hypotheses; the units are final answers, not probes. Older models; samples are independent, not sequential.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the closest direct test that an explicit stop rule beats a fixed budget at equal cost. It suggests the S3 stop test should be a cheap coded confidence check on the leading hypothesis, not an LLM judgement. A test on open-ended probes is still missing.

source: Liu & Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Reasoning models often reach their final answer well before the end of the chain of thought. Stopping when the answer has stayed the same over several checks saves tokens on easy tasks and is unstable on hard ones.
numbers: Five benchmarks, five open-weight reasoning models. On math, models converge after about 60% of reasoning steps. Answer-consistency stop cuts tokens by over 40% on NaturalQuestions while accuracy rises. Learn-to-Stop (a trained probe on activations) cuts tokens 46.2% for R1-Qwen-7B and 47.7% for 32B on NQ.
limits: Unsupervised stop signals were less stable on MATH-500 and GPQA, the harder sets (authors). Needs partial answers; the trained probe needs activations, so it cannot be used through a plain API.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: stop-on-convergence works where tasks are easy and is unreliable where reasoning is deep. A stop rule for S3 should be paired with a minimum probe count and a check that the leading hypothesis is not stuck on a wrong answer.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025, ICLR) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design. Instead of enumerating hypotheses, it asks the LLM to sample a set of compatible solutions and estimates the expected information gain over that sample. This beats letting the LLM reason in question space. Open (many-answer) questions can be more informative than yes/no ones.
numbers: 20 Questions game: N=20 sampled animals per step, 10 rounds, 15 ground-truth animals, 5 run seeds, 25 evaluation seeds. EIG-uniform clearly beat implicit and implicit-ToT questioning; EIG-logprobs was clearly worse than EIG-uniform (the LLM's own sample probabilities are biased). Code task: 4 extra requirements, 48 tasks, 3 runs; EIG strategies gave higher pass rates, with a smaller gap for stronger models (Llama3-8B, GPT-3.5, Llama3-70B, GPT-4o-mini tested).
limits: The authors list two limits: no rule for when to stop asking, and extra LLM calls (they argue the cost is small). The hypotheses are LLM-generated, so the set is only as open as the LLM's imagination. The gap shrinks with stronger models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for an open hypothesis space, sample hypotheses from the LLM, filter them against the evidence so far, treat the samples as equally likely, and compute the gain in code. Do not use the LLM's own token probabilities as weights. A stop rule is explicitly missing here (gap 1 stays open).

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2024, ICLR) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: An LLM judges which learnable tasks are also interesting and weights task choice by it. Learning progress alone and uniform sampling are the controls. A control that treats novelty as embedding-cluster distance is also described. OMNI beat uniform and learning progress alone on Crafter.
numbers: Crafter (15 tasks) with PPO agents, about 33 h per run on one A10 GPU; BabyAI about 60 h. OMNI gave higher average task success and learned more tasks than uniform sampling or learning progress alone (the numbers are in figures, not in the text I read).
limits: The interest judge is an LLM trained on human text, so it carries human tastes (circular, as the earlier critique said). No explicit noisy-TV test with unlearnable distractors was found in the text read; learning progress is the guard against unlearnable noise.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly: an LLM interesting filter on top of a learnability signal beats the learnability signal alone. It is not shown to beat raw novelty at equal tokens on unlearnable distractors. Best design: learnability (gain falling over repeated probes) plus an LLM relevance filter.

source: Handa, Gal, Pavlick, Goodman, Andreas, Tamkin, Li (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: The LM proposes the features and writes the questions; a Bayesian experimental-design step picks the next question by expected information gain over the user's preferences. In user studies this beat LM-only elicitation.
numbers: Six user-study conditions with 39-48 users each (48 for LM questions + OPEN predictions; 44 for OPEN questions + LM predictions). Metric: time-integrated delta accuracy. OPEN pairwise questions beat LM-only pairwise questions. Open-ended LM questions beat pairwise ones when scored by an LM but could not use the Bayesian predictor.
limits: Preference learning, not reasoning. The benefit shrinks when the LM is also the predictor. Per-condition effect sizes were not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the LLM-writes-candidates, code-scores-information split works with real people. Explicit tracking of the belief state is what the LM-only methods lack.

source: Austin, Suleman, Cheung (2026, COLM) Semantic Bandits: In-Context Exploration-Exploitation is Biased by Semantic Priors
finding: Action labels change exploration. Labels that suggest a good option cut exploration: this helps if the label fits the reward and badly hurts if it does not. Negative rewards trigger more exploration than the same positive rewards. Even Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, a reasoning model, still showed semantic priors.
numbers: 3 arms, normalised cumulative regret. Models: OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B (thinking limited to 150 tokens), Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite (thinking unlimited). OLMo barely explored unless told it was a bandit task; Gemini explored fast and matched the reward-normative pattern on most tasks. In pilots Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B did not display sufficient exploration; Qwen3-14B matched 32B.
limits: Three models, 3-arm tasks. The 8B result is a pilot remark, not a table. The reasoning-token limit differs between models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 7: probe labels and reward sign shape exploration, so S3 should present probes under neutral labels and in a fixed reward frame. Rough size floor: near 8B, exploration behaviour is too weak to count on.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2023/2024) Active Preference Inference using Language Models and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: The LLM proposes yes/no questions; code scores each by expected entropy reduction over which product the user wants. The two objectives (entropy and expected model change) are equal in this setting. Three questions of the scored method beat four questions of the plain LLM.
numbers: 150 shopping tasks of 10 products each, GPT-4 as asker and as simulated user, 8 candidate questions sampled per step. Binary reward: entropy-reduction LLM clearly better than vanilla and ReAct baselines for more than one question; after 3 questions it already surpassed the baselines after 4. Information per question is largest in the first three; at the 4th question little information is left.
limits: Closed set of 10 items and yes/no answers only. The authors say open-ended questions need a Monte Carlo approximation and that this is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 3: shows the information gain falling toward zero as the closed set empties (a natural stop point) and that the number of candidate questions (8) is a cheap lever. The open-set approximation is still untested here.

source: Berdica, Acero, Ipsen, Zehtabi, Cashmore, Veloso (2026) When Do We Need LLMs? A Diagnostic for Language-Driven Bandits
finding: Uncertainty estimated from repeated LLM inference (LLMP-UCB) works, but plain numerical bandits on text embeddings match or beat LLM-based solutions at far lower cost. A geometric diagnostic of the arm embeddings says when LLM reasoning is worth it.
numbers: Contextual bandits with text plus numeric context. Number-level results were not read; abstract and introduction only.
limits: Contextual bandits, not hypothesis testing. Only the abstract and introduction were read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and 1: counting and uncertainty bookkeeping should live in code; call the LLM only where language adds information. Supports a skip-the-scaffold test.

source: Yang & Chen (2025) In-Context Curiosity: Distilling Exploration for Decision-Pretrained Transformers on Bandit Tasks
finding: A curiosity bonus based on the error of a reward predictor, added during pretraining of a bandit transformer, reduces the loss in robustness when test variance rises, mainly when pretraining data are not diverse.
numbers: Gaussian bandits. The benefit shrinks as test variance rises and the new model converges toward the baseline's regret. Proof-of-concept scale.
limits: Training-time method on small transformers, not a prompt scaffold. The authors call the results preliminary. Prediction error is exactly the noisy-TV-prone signal.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. A prediction-error curiosity bonus helps only when data are narrow; no use for a prompt-only agent.
